analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal charter for online lenders exempt from state rate caps, with no federal rate limit.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, it stayed there until the Congress ended in January 2015, though a Senate Banking subcommittee held a hearing in March 2014.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let online lenders get a special federal charter to lend to people who can't get loans from banks — the unbanked and people with poor credit — over the internet, nationwide. The trade at the heart of it: a chartered lender would no longer have to follow any state's interest rate caps or licensing rules, and the bill forbids federal regulators from setting any interest rate limit either. It does include some borrower protections — no 30-day-or-shorter loans, no loans due in one lump-sum payday-style payment, a check that borrowers can repay, a cap of $5,000 on unsecured loans, and one free extended repayment plan a year.
analysis.who_benefits: Online nonbank lenders gain a nationwide charter free of state rate caps and licensing regimes, with no federal cap replacing them. Underserved consumers and small businesses gain a new online source of credit with some written safeguards, though the bill's own text concedes that for these borrowers the cost, measured as an annual rate, will be much higher than for other borrowers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Online small-dollar lenders; underserved borrowers seeking credit

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federal charter so internet lenders can serve underserved consumers and small businesses nationwide without brick-and-mortar locations.

Chartered lenders are freed from state licensing laws and from state laws that would 'prevent or significantly interfere' with their operations, including rate restrictions, under a preemption standard the creditor can challenge in court.

Includes borrower safeguards: no loans of 30 days or less, no loan requiring a single lump-sum repayment, no prepayment penalties, an ability-to-repay requirement, a $5,000 cap on unsecured consumer loans, and at least one free extended repayment plan per year for borrowers who can't pay a loan under 120 days.
Requires lenders to disclose the true cost of a loan — all interest, fees, and charges — as a dollar amount and as a percentage of the principal, and to provide financial counseling information.

analysis.who_pays: Borrowers bear the cost: with no federal rate cap and state caps not applying to chartered lenders, high-cost small loans become available nationwide at prices no state chose to allow. State regulators and state attorneys general lose much of their authority over chartered lenders, and state-licensed lenders that still obey state rate caps face competitors who don't.

drawbacks.text: The bill bars the Comptroller of the Currency and the consumer bureau from regulating the price of these loans in any way — no usury limit, no cap on interest, fees, or other charges.

It instructs regulators that a loan may not be presumed unfair or abusive solely because its rates are much higher than loans to people with good credit, and the findings concede the cost 'will be considerably higher' and, as an annual percentage rate, 'much higher.'

For loans of one year or less, the bill replaces the standard Truth in Lending Act APR disclosure with a dollar cost and a percentage of principal — a format that makes these loans look cheaper next to the APR figure on longer loans.
Chartered lenders are largely exempt from state consumer-credit laws, so in any state that has capped rates to protect borrowers, those protections would not apply to federally chartered lenders.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Access to credit for people banks won't serve is a real need, and the bill is not a blank check — the ability-to-repay rule, the ban on payday-style lump-sum loans and sub-30-day loans, and the extended repayment plan are genuine protections. But the design removes the one thing that has traditionally limited the price of these loans, state rate caps, while explicitly forbidding any federal price limit and softening the cost disclosure. The bill's own text admits the loans will carry much higher annual rates. What's left is a nationwide market for high-cost small loans where the safeguards are structural but the price is unregulated.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and never moved again in the House; the only action after that was a hearing in a Senate Banking subcommittee in March 2014, and the Congress ended in January 2015 without either chamber voting on it.

narrative.text: Introduced April 15, 2013 by Rep. Blaine Luetkemeyer with Rep. Gregory Meeks as co-lead, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services.
The bill drew 18 cosponsors, 10 Republicans and 8 Democrats.
On March 26, 2014, the Senate Banking Committee's Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Protection held a hearing on the subject, but no chamber ever brought the bill to a vote.
The bill died in committee when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State rate-cap laws and the borrowers they protect stayed intact, since no chartered high-cost lending market was created; online lenders got a hearing and bipartisan cosponsors but no nationwide charter.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: State rate caps and the borrowers they protect

industries.industry: Nonbank small-dollar consumer lenders (online installment and payday lenders)
industries.note: The bill creates a national charter letting these lenders operate in every state without obeying state rate caps or licensing, and forbids any federal rate cap — the profit model depends on charging borrowers rates far above what state limits allow. The bill's own findings argue state rate laws 'severely' restrict these products.

industries.industry: State consumer-credit regulators and state-licensed lenders
industries.note: Chartered lenders are exempt from state licensing, office-location rules, and laws that significantly interfere with their powers, so state authority shrinks. State-licensed lenders that remain under state caps would face rivals free of those caps.

The findings say banks' high costs and strict credit standards keep them from serving these borrowers profitably, and the bill restricts chartered lenders to serving markets banks don't reach; banks could also partner or affiliate with chartered lenders.
